title: Ad-Duha: the morning
hookLine: your Lord has not left you, and what comes after is better (93:1–5)
tomorrow: Ad-Duha: the orphan and the asker

cards: You text someone you love, and they don't answer. An hour. A day.
A week. And your mind fills the silence: they're angry, they're done with me, I did something wrong. Silence is where the worst stories get written.
Something like that happened to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. In the early years of revelation, the verses stopped coming. Days passed, then more.
People around him noticed, and some were cruel about it. The silence ended with this surah, and its first word is light.

teach.b: Sahih al-Bukhari records that the Prophet fell ill and didn't rise for prayer at night for a few nights, and a woman taunted him that his companion, meaning the one who brought the revelation, had abandoned him.
Reports differ on the length of the pause and on who said what. They share the silence, and the sting. Then came Surah ninety-three.

In Pickthall's translation: By the morning hours And by the night when it is stillest, Thy Lord hath not forsaken thee nor doth He hate thee, And verily the latter portion will be better for thee than the former, And verily thy Lord will give unto thee so that thou wilt be content.
Duha is the bright part of the morning, when the sun is well up and the day is warm.

teach.h: BY THE MORNING, BY THE STILL NIGHT.
teach.b: Two oaths: the bright morning and the still night.

In the surah, both belong to the same Lord. The night didn't mean the morning was gone; it was just night. Then the direct answer to the fear: your Lord has not left you, and He is not angry with you.
Two sentences, answering exactly the two worst stories silence tells. Then a promise: the later will be better for you than the earlier.

teach.h: THE LATTER BETTER THAN THE FORMER.
teach.b: Commentators read it two ways: the rest of his life better than its beginning, and the next life better than this one.
And a last line: your Lord will give you until you are content. Not a lecture. Something closer to a hand on the shoulder.

how: Many Muslims turn to Surah ad-Duha in times of sadness or waiting; the mid-morning voluntary prayer, salat ad-duha, shares its name with the surah's first word.

o: the stillness of the night after prayer
the first light just before the sun rises
the bright part of the morning, sun well up

games.q: what's inside the surah — tap the pairs.
p: the bright part of the morning

s: the revelation to the Prophet once paused
and a woman taunted him that he'd been abandoned (Bukhari).
the surah scolds the Prophet for worrying
it reassures him: your Lord hath not forsaken thee.
all reports agree exactly how long the pause lasted
reports differ on the length and on who said what.

games.q: the revelation has gone quiet, and someone says your Lord has abandoned you. what are the surah's first words of answer?
o: your Lord hath not forsaken thee nor doth He hate thee
games.why: it answers the two worst stories silence tells, directly (93:3), after oaths by the morning and the still night.

practice: Think of a silence in your life right now, something you're waiting on, and notice the story your mind is writing into it.
Then set that story down, picture the morning after a long night, the light getting warm, and hold one hope that begins: later, I hope.

wordCard.voice: Ad-Duha. The bright morning, the name of Surah ninety-three, which says: your Lord has not left you, and the later is better. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the bright morning, when the sun is high; also the name of the mid-morning prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: the later is better. Even a long silence can end in morning. See you tomorrow.
